title: One Step Diffusion via Shortcut Models

nodes.text: Shortcut models are a family of generative models that condition the network not only on the current noise level/timestep but also on a desired step size d, allowing the model to jump ahead in the denoising process and produce samples in one or multiple steps with a single network and single training phase.
nodes.evidence: Shortcut models condition the network not only on the current noise level but also on the desired step size, allowing the model to skip ahead in the generation process.

nodes.text: Shortcut models are a generalization of flow-matching models to larger step sizes: flow-matching learns only the instantaneous velocity, while shortcut models additionally learn to make larger jumps, with the shortcut becoming equivalent to the flow as the step size d goes to 0.
nodes.evidence: Shortcut models can thus be seen as a generalization of flow-matching models to larger step sizes... At d -> 0, the shortcut is equivalent to the flow.

nodes.text: Unlike distillation and consistency models, shortcut models are trained end-to-end in a single training run without a separate distillation phase, multiple networks, or a careful learning schedule/warmup.
nodes.evidence: Unlike distillation or consistency models, shortcut models are trained in a single training run without a schedule.

nodes.text: Training uses a self-consistency property: one shortcut step of size 2d equals the concatenation of two consecutive shortcut steps of size d, i.e. s(xt,t,2d) = s(xt,t,d)/2 + s(x'_{t+d},t,d)/2, used to build bootstrap targets for d>0 while the flow-matching loss serves as the base case for d=0.
nodes.evidence: one shortcut step equals two consecutive shortcut steps of half the size: s(xt, t, 2d) = s(xt, t, d)/2 + s(x't+d, t, d)/2

nodes.text: Shortcut models perform self-distillation during training, eliminating the need for a separate distillation step.
nodes.evidence: Shortcut models can be seen as performing self-distillation during training time, and thus do not require a separate distillation step

nodes.text: Naive diffusion and flow-matching models fail at one-step generation for multi-modal data because at t=0 the predicted velocity points toward the dataset mean, so even at the optimum of the flow-matching objective one-step generation fails.
nodes.evidence: even at the optimum of the flow matching objective, one step generation will fail for any multi-modal data distribution.

nodes.text: On CelebA-HQ and ImageNet-256 under fixed architecture and compute, shortcut models match or exceed two-stage distillation methods in few- and one-step settings and significantly outperform previous end-to-end methods across inference budgets, while many-step quality matches baseline diffusion models.
nodes.evidence: Shortcut models match or exceed the distillation methods that require multiple training phases and significantly outperform previous end-to-end methods across inference budgets.

nodes.text: Shortcut models consistently produce higher quality samples than prior approaches such as consistency models and reflow across a wide range of sampling step budgets.
nodes.evidence: shortcut models consistently produce higher quality samples than previous approaches, such as consistency models and reflow.

nodes.text: Training a shortcut model requires only about 16% more compute than an equivalent base diffusion model, achieved by combining a ratio of (1-k) empirical flow-matching targets with k self-consistency targets (k=1/4).
nodes.evidence: we can reduce the training cost of a shortcut model to be roughly only ~16% more than that of an equivalent diffusion model

nodes.text: Applied to robotic control as shortcut policies replacing diffusion policies, shortcut models maintain comparable performance at an order-of-magnitude lower inference cost.
nodes.evidence: shortcut models maintain comparable performance under an order-of-magnitude lower inference cost.

nodes.text: Weight decay is used to stabilize early training because near initialization the self-consistency bootstrap targets are largely noise; proper weight decay removes the need for discretization schedules or careful warmups.
nodes.evidence: We find that proper weight decay causes these issues to disappear, and enables us to bypass the need for discretization schedules or careful warmups.

nodes.text: Classifier-free guidance is applied only when evaluating at d=0 (small step size) and forgone at larger steps, since CFG's linear approximation is error-prone for large jumps; the CFG scale must be fixed before training.
nodes.evidence: We therefore use CFG when evaluating the shortcut model at d = 0 but forgo it elsewhere.
